claims.text: Explicitly modeling defect structures and oxygen scattering will improve electrical-conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr relative to perfect-crystal analytical methods.
The improvement will apply in both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr naturally contains non-idealities relevant to electrical transport.
A specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen represents realistic impurity effects in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Point defects and oxygen produce local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen and other defect sites modify the local electronic structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-induced lattice and electronic-structure changes alter electron scattering.
Impurity scattering is the relevant low-temperature transport regime from 0 to 200 K.
Electron–phonon and impurity interactions dominate transport from 300 to 1200 K.
Adding defect-scattering terms and defect-modified band structures will better represent electron transport in nonideal HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model can capture experimental conductivity deviations missed by idealized analytical models.
The proposed model will predict conductivity within roughly 10% of experiment across both temperature regimes.
The proposed model will predict modestly higher low-temperature conductivity than perfect-crystal models because it includes realistic impurity scattering.
The proposed model will predict an adjusted high-temperature conductivity dependence relative to perfect-crystal models.
Perfect, defect-free analytical models generally have larger discrepancies from experiment when defects are present.
The proposed model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed model's claimed temperature applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Inert-atmosphere testing prevents additional oxidation during conductivity measurements.
